question: On 14 March 2024, YouTube made a unilateral decision to remove a video on MEP Sergio Berlato’s channel. The video in question documented the event ‘Pretendiamo Verità e Giustizia’ (‘Pretend truth and justice’) held in Bassano del Grappa (VI) on 9 March 2024, which was attended by 2 500 people and internationally renowned speakers, including doctors, scientists, journalists, committee representatives and MEPs.

The platform justified the decision by saying: ‘Our team has reviewed your content and, unfortunately, we think it violates our medical misinformation policy’. Given that there was no misinformation shared at this event but rather only evidence of what happened during the socalled COVID-19 pandemic, YouTube’s censorship is discriminatory and unfounded. In view of the above: 1.

Does the Commission consider it appropriate to outsource the role of censoring the opinions of scientists, doctors, publishers, politicians, victims and citizens to web giants, operating, outside the framework of national and international legislation, on the basis of ‘community standards’ set behind closed doors?
Does it believe that web giants are neutral in their mediation of the content published on their platforms?
answer: Since the adoption of the Digital Services Act (DSA) (1), content moderation practices of social media platforms are subject to due diligence obligations for a safer online space while ensuring transparency, accountability and freedom of expression and information, to the benefit of EU citizens.

For example, the providers of such platforms must include in their terms and conditions clear, user-friendly information on any restriction they might impose on users or the content they share, and they must act in a diligent, objective and proportionate manner in applying those restrictions, with due regard to the fundamental rights of users.
Moreover, the DSA requires such providers to explain their decisions to users in a clear and specific statement of reasons and offer an effective internal complaint-handling system for free.

All these procedural obligations and safeguards are intended to make content moderation practices of online platforms more responsible and transparent, but this does not mean that the providers of online platforms can determine the scope of fundamental rights, such as the freedom of expression and information, in the EU, which is ultimately a task entrusted to the courts.

The Commission is not able to comment on individual cases, which are under the responsibility of national authorities. The Commission has exclusive jurisdiction on direct enforcement vis-à-vis designated very large online platforms, like YouTube and, in case of a systematic breach of the DSA such as the requirement of objective content moderation, it can investigate the matter and may impose a fine.
